blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — oral potassium chloride administration
stem: A client is prescribed potassium chloride extended-release tablets. Which statement shows correct understanding of administration?

options.A: I will take each dose with meals and a full glass of water or other liquid and avoid taking it on an empty stomach.
options.B: I will chew the extended-release tablet thoroughly with each meal so the potassium is released more quickly into the stomach.
options.C: I will take each dose on an empty stomach because food increases gastrointestinal irritation from potassium chloride.
options.D: I will crush the extended-release tablet into food because crushing improves absorption and reduces the chance of gastrointestinal injury.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling directs patients to take potassium chloride extended-release tablets with meals and with a full glass of water or other liquid and not on an empty stomach because of gastric irritation risk. The label also directs patients not to crush, chew, or suck the tablets. Therefore A is correct. B and D disrupt the extended-release dosage form, and C reverses the food instruction.
educational_objective: Administer potassium chloride extended-release tablets with meals and adequate liquid, not on an empty stomach, and do not crush or chew the dosage form.
source_document_title: Potassium Chloride Extended-Release Tablets, USP — Prescribing Information
source_locator: Information for Patients and Dosage and Administration: take each dose with meals and a full glass of water or other liquid; do not take on an empty stomach; do not crush, chew, or suck the tablets.
source_claim_supported: Potassium chloride ER tablets should be taken with meals and liquid, not on an empty stomach, and should not be crushed or chewed.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: educate clients about medications and administer oral medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Removed isolated absolute-word cueing and rewrote all choices as full administration statements.
Added the label-supported do-not-crush/chew constraint to make distractors clinically plausible.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches current labeling. B and D improperly alter the ER tablet; C reverses the meal instruction. No second defensible answer remains.
